entity: Patton, Boggs, Blow, Verrill, Brand & May
role: legal counsel for International Snowmobile Industry Association
stance_basis: letter supports ORRV/snowmobile use but demands differentiated classification, revised BLM policy, and improved safety regulations
summary: Patton, Boggs, Blow, Verrill, Brand & May, as counsel for the International Snowmobile Industry Association, submitted a detailed comment letter arguing that the Draft Environmental Statement fails to adequately differentiate between types of ORRVs (especially snowmobiles vs. other vehicles), improperly proposes reversing BLM's open-use policy, and contains inequitable and poorly tailored safety regulations. The firm conditionally supports the regulatory effort but urges significant revisions to protect snowmobile recreational opportunities while achieving genuine environmental protection.
complaint_summary: The firm argues on behalf of ISIA that the Draft Environmental Statement fails to differentiate between ORRV types (particularly snowmobiles), improperly proposes reversing BLM's open-use policy, contains inequitable and poorly designed safety regulations, and inadequately addresses interagency coordination and state/local land programs.

statement.text:
The following comments are submitted, on behalf of *
the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) in response to the Notice of Availability of Draft Environmental Statement [Int Des 72-58] published in Federal Register Vol. 37, No. 107 on June 2, 1972.
Virtually all major manufacturers of snowmobiles and related products. In this capacity, the Association has been actively interested in the development of federal policies affecting Off-Road Recreational Vehicles (ORRVs) and in addition to its consideration of the above referenced Draft Statement, has carefully reviewed and considered the Department's OERV Task Force Study released in April of 1972. Since the Task Force Study is an important background document for the Draft Statement, the comments set forth below are directed to such Study as well as to the Draft Statement itself.
* See attached membership list.
12

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Two .
At the outset, we should like to emphasize the fact that neither the National Environmental Policy Act nor Executive Order 11644 in any way supersedes or supplants the Secretary's responsibility, under the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963 to assure adequate outdoor recreation resources and to take prompt action "to conserve, develop and utilize, such resources for the benefit of the American people."
with this factor in mind, and since ORRV use is recognized as a significant and beneficial outdoor recreational acticity, it is clear that, in promulgating regulations in implementation of the Executive Order, the Department must strike an appropriate balance between its stewardship responsibility under the Order and its general obligation to develop and utilize its land resources in such a manner as to promote broad public recreational use.
Such a balance can only be achieved by a detailed classification of ORRV's, ORRV uses and land resource categories together with a realistic appraisal of demonstrable and significant adverse environmental impacts resulting from specific ORRV uses on specific types of lands. The Draft Statement totally fails to isolate and identify any specific demonstrable environmental impact of ORRV use. It is clear that further study is required and that, properly done, this project will be of significant duration. Thus careful planning is necessary to assure that recreational opportunities are not unduly restricted pending completion of the final classification.
Against this general background, the Association's specific comments are as follows:

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Three
I. Adequate Differentiation Between Classes
of ORRVs and ORRV Uses -
We are surprised and disappointed to note that neither the Draft Statement (and the proposed regulations discussed therein) nor the Task Force Study's recommendations make any reference to any intention to give consideration to varying types of ORRVs and ORRV uses in establishing the final regulations under the Executive Order. We fail to see how any regulatory program can properly balance the need for minimization of adverse environmental impact against the need to promote recreational use without carefully classifying the possible impacts of the varying types of ORRV use and tailoring the regulatory approach to take into account the specific requirements of each type of vehicle.*
This failure to differentiate between ORRV classifications would be especially discriminatory and unjustified in respect to its impact on opportunities for snowmobile use since the snowmobile's impact on the environment, as compared to that of other ORRV types, is insignificant.
Snowmobile operation takes place in the winter when the land is dormant and well covered by a protective blanket of snow and the snowmobile is designed to be supported on wide skis and a flexible track of sufficient width to provide flotation on the snow. Because of this design, the snowmobile exerts a pressure
* The failure to take such factors into account would result, for example, in the absurd conclusion that snowmobile and trail bike use must be permitted in all camping areas where vehicular "campers" are allowed.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Four
of only .40 to .50 p.s.i. on the ground beneath it (as compared to the approximate 2.75 p.s.i. exerted by an average man standing and the approximate 10 p.s.i. exerted by an average man riding a motorcycle).
Because of these factors snowmobiles, during the winter period in which they are designed to be used, can be operated without significant risk of environmental harm except in certain limited areas which are especially delicate or especially susceptible to environmental harm.* The foregoing statement does not hold true for all ORRV classifications and there is no doubt that, in the winter snowmobiles can properly be used, without environmental risk, in many areas which should. clearly be closed to use by other types of ORRV's during other seasons of the year (e.g. trail bikes on grasslands in the early spring). Failure to distinguish between the environmental impact of snowmobile use and that of other ORRV uses will result in the unavailability of important Outdoor Recreational Resources for snowmobile use even though there is no relevant environmental basis for such unavailability. Such a result is not only manifestly unfair but is also in direct contravention of the Outdoor Recreation Act's mandate to "utilize" these resources "for the benefit of the American people."
* 
Reference is made to the Report on the Ecological Impact of Snowmobiles on Public Lands prepared by the Editors of Popular Science Magazine. Copies are being forwarded under separate cover.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Five
II. Adequate Differentiation Between Types of Land Resources Under Department of Interior Jurisdiction -
Historically, there have been definite distinctions in the characteristics of lands managed by the separate Bureaus within the Department of Interior. In response to those distinctions, each of the Bureaus has developed a regulatory approach which is tailored to the peculiar requirements of the lands under its jurisdiction. Consider, for example, the following historical approaches.
A. The Park Service (NPS) -
NPS is charged under its enabling statutes with the administration of National Parks, National Monuments and National Historic Sites. These land areas were added to the national park system by specific congressional action based on their unique scenic, natural, historical or archeological characteristics and, in general, receive high density use by the public. With respect to these areas, the enabling legislation emphasizes the Park Service's responsibility for conservation and protection of unique natural values and the Park Service has adequate staff resources for the fulfillment of this responsibility.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Six
NPS is also charged with the administration of "recreational areas" which, like the land areas referenced above, are designated by specific Congressional enactment, generally have somewhat unique natural characteristics and receive high density public use. Unlike the areas noted above, the primary purpose of recreational areas is that of public recreation.
Based on its experience in administering the above described areas and in light of the Congressional emphasis on the stewardship function and the high density use which is common in such areas, NPS has determined that ORRV use can best be regulated by confining such use to specifically designated areas. In light of the Park Service's substantial personnel resources, this regulatory approach has apparently been enforceable. This "prohibited except where specifically permitted" regulatory approach would apparently be carried forward by the regulations under the Executive Order. In light of the unique characteristics of the land areas involved, the Congressional emphasis on preservation, the high density use and the existence of adequate enforcement personnel, the Association agrees that, with respect to the lands described above, the aforementioned regulatory approach is appropriate. It should be emphasized, however, that with regard to recreational areas, their primary purpose is recreation and thus great emphasis should be placed on the establishment of trails and designated areas wherever significant

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Seven
and irreversible environmental impact would not result. With respect to the parks, national monuments and national historic sites, we note that the encouragement of enjoyment by recreational users is a congressionally established goal which should be actively pursued wherever compatible with the steward-ship or environmental preservation functions of the NPS with respect to such lands.
B. Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife (BSFW) -
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BSFW is responsible for the management of some 30 million acres of public land and is charged with the primary responsibility of the protection and perpetuation of wildlife resources. Historically, BSFW has followed a fairly restrictive use policy similar to that of the National Park Service described above. The Association is in agreement as to the applicability of the "prohibited except where specifically permitted" regulatory approach when applied to BSFW lands. However, it is again emphasized that the Secretary does have a responsibility for promoting recreational use of this land to the extent that such use will not adversely affect environmental values. Accordingly, BSFW should be encouraged to actively review its land areas with a view towards designation of ORRV areas and trails wherever possible under the aforesaid criterion.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eight
C. Bureau of Land Management
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BLM is responsible for the management of approximately 452 million acres of public land. In general, the BLM lands do not possess the unique scenic, natural, historic or archeological characteristics present in the NPS lands nor do they generally function as important wildlife conservation centers as is the case with the BSFW lands. Public use of BLM lands is generally low density in nature and BLM has limited personnel available for the purpose of enforcing any regulation of ORRV use. Based on these factors. the historical BLM policy with respect to ORRV use has been to permit such use in all areas except those which are closed to such use for a specific reason. The Department's proposed implementation of the Executive Order would apparently reverse this policy and would provide for the confining of ORRV use to areas and trails designated as open to such use. Even in such open areas, ORRV use would be subject to certain controls.
while the Association does not disagree with the goal of imposing reasonable restrictions on ORRV use in any area of the BLM lands, it does strongly disagree with the Department's apparent intention to reverse BLM's historical approach with respect to the classification of lands. For the reasons set forth below, such reversal is not only unwise from an environmental

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Nine
point of view but is also in direct contravention of the Secretary's responsibilities under the 1963 Outdoor Recreation Act. In our opinion, such reversal of policy would have the following aspects:
Indefinite and Unjustified Limitation of Available Outdoor Recreation Resources Pending Completion of Classification - BLM, as noted above, is responsible for the management of over 452 million acres of public land which land is widely dispersed and of highly diverse characteristics. Given existing staff resources, it would be expected that the envisaged classification of all BLM lands into that which is open for use and that which is closed to use will be a project of at least several years in duration. Since no significant amount of public lands has yet been classified as opened to ORRV use, the effect of the proposed sudden reversal in policy will be to close all BLM lands to ORRV use until the above-referenced classification scheme is completed. Thus, the proposed scheme of regulation would presume that ORRV use - a beneficial recreational activity - is environmentally objectionable until the contrary is proven. It is submitted that such policy is not reasonably calculated to promote and develop recreational resources for the American people. To the contrary, it seems more reasonably calculated to have the opposite result. The appropriateness

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Ten
of such a policy is clearly questionable in light of the manifest Congressional intention set forth in the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963. There is no justification for this contravention of Congressional policy either by reference to the characteristics of BLM lands or by any demonstration of environmental damages which have resulted from the historical implementation of the present open use policy.
2. Concentration of ORRV Use Within the

Specifically Defined Areas  As noted above, ORRV use
on BLM lands is now widely dispersed and it is clear that
such low density use tends to have a less significant\nenvironmental impact than high density use in designated
areas. The effect of the reversal in policy referenced
above would be, especially in the earlier years of the
policy's implementation, to concentrate ORRV use in such
areas as have been specifically classified as open. Thus,
with respect to BLM lands, the proposed reversal in policy
would not protect the environment but, by concentration of
ORRV use in certain areas, would tend to heighten any impact
which such use might have.
3. Placing of Impossible Burdens Upon BLM

Enforcement Personnel  As indicated above, BLM has limited staff resources and, even assuming that such staff is adequate to evaluate and classify all of the 452 million

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eleven
acres of public domain land under BLM jurisdiction, it is ludicrous to expect that staff to post and deny public access to all of such lands except those that are specifically classified as open. If, on the other hand, BLM is permitted to follow its existing policy of focusing on the specific areas where adverse environmental impact is likely to occur and devoting its resources towards the exclusion of ORRV users from those specified areas, there is at least some hope of achieving an effective scheme of regulation which will be adhered to by the users.
Compared to these apparent and significant adverse impacts of reversal of existing BLM policy, the only advantage of such reversal of which we are aware is that of achieving uniform policy for all lands under Interior jurisdiction. Such uniformity is a mere matter of administrative convenience. It is not dictated either by the Executive Order or by any other Interior enabling statute. Elimination of the positive environmental and recreational benefits of the existing regulatory approach as a mere matter of administrative convenience is clearly inappropriate and we would therefore suggest that the Department reconsider its apparent intention to deviate from ELM's existing land management policy with respect to ORRV use.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Twelve
D. Bureau of Reclamation Lands - The Bureau of Reclamation Lands are similar in characteristic to those under the management of BLM. Historically, the Bureau of Reclamation has followed an "open except where prohibited" policy similar to that of BLM. For the reasons discussed above with respect to the BLM lands we believe that the existing regulatory approach of the Bureau of Reclamation should be preserved and that departure from this historic approach would have adverse impacts both from the environmental point of view and the point of view of available outdoor recreational resources.
Based on the foregoing, it is our opinion that the Draft Environmental Impact Statement and the proposed regulations discussed therein give inadequate attention to the varying characteristics of the lands administered by the several Bureaus. This approach appears to be in direct contravention of the Task Force Study's recommendations that, in developing the new regulations consideration be given to existing regulations and specific land classifications. It is our opinion that the significantly divergent characteristics of the several land categories require significant variations in regulatory approach. These factors should be taken into account in finalizing the regulations in implementation of the Executive Order.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Thirteen
III. Safety and Operating Requirements -
While we are somewhat doubtful as to whether the National Environmental Policy Act gives the President and the Department legal authority to promulgate safety related requirements for ORRV use, the Association is not opposed to the imposition of reasonable regulations in this area. However, perhaps because of the absence of clear authority, the proposed safely related regulations are inequitable in that they impose the entire burden of compliance on the consumer although, in fairness, at least a portion of the compliance responsibility should rest on the vehicle manufacturer.
Moreover, a review of the proposed safety criteria indicates that they are not based on a careful consideration of the precise characteristics of the types of vehicles to be covered. As an example, consider the proposed requirement that persons operating ORRVs have valid permits to operate a motor vehicle. In the case of snowmobiles there is no demonstrated correlation between the ability to pass an automobile or motor-cycle drivers test and the ability to safely operate a snowmobile. In the absence of such a demonstrated correlation the proposed regulation is clearly improper in that it excludes many persons from the recreational opportunities of snowmobile operation without any showing of a safety related basis for such exclusion and thus the major snowmobiling states have seen fit to

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Fourteen
specifically eliminate any connection between snowmobile operation and motor vehicle licensing. The Association does support programs designed to educate snowmobile operators and to require youthful snowmobile operators to obtain safety certificates. A further indication of the failure to consider the specific nature of the types of vehicles regulated is the requirement for "spark arrestors" on snowmobiles. In virtually all states where snowmobile equipment requirements have been adopted, it has been recognized that, because of the environment in which snowmobiles operate, the spark arrestor requirement is inapplicable to snowmobiles.
Department's proposed regulations insofar as they pertain to safety, together with the generally rudimentary and superficial character of such regulations in their presently proposed form, point up the need for additional legislative action granting the Department authority to regulate the safety characteristics of ORRVs used on public lands. The Association would support responsible legislation of this type.
IV. The Department's Responsibilities Vis-a-Vis
Other Land Responsible Federal Agencies -
Executive Order 1164 stresses the need for "a unified Federal policy toward the use of [ORRVs] on public lands" and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963 directs the Secretary to "promote coordination of Federal plans and activities generally relating to Outdoor Recreation." Pursuant to these directives,

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Fifteen
the Draft Statement and the proposed regulations discussed therein do direct the Assistant Secretary -- Program Policy to provide "liaison" and "technical assistance" to other land responsible Federal agencies in an effort to coordinate ORRV regulation. Such "liaison" and "technical assistance", however, would appear likely to fall considerably short of the kind of close interagency cooperative effort which is necessary to obtain the joint regulatory approach which is necessary if agency actions are to be truly coordinated. We would suggest that the Executive Order can best be implemented by carrying forward the interagency task force approach followed in development of the Task Force Study in an effort to develop joint regulations implementing the Executive Order. We would, of course, anticipate that Interior would be the lead agency in this task force. If legislation is necessary to implement this approach, we would support such legislation.
V. The Department's Responsibilities Vis-a-Vis
State, Local Governments and Private Lands -
We note with approval the indication in the Draft
Statement that the Department intends to devote some effort
towards assisting states, local governments and private organizations and individuals in developing areas and facilities for
ORRV use. It should be emphasized, however, that, to a very
major extent, the real effectiveness of any national program

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Sixteen
7
to reconcile ORRV use with the need for environmental protection will depend on the program's effectiveness with respect to the state, local and private lands where a very significant portion of the ORRV use occurs. In this connection, we question whether "technical assistance" is enough. We see a definite need for the Department to take an active role in the development of a nationwide federal-state program for the proper regulation of ORRV use on all lands. As a necessary adjunct to this program, we believe that some consideration might be given to the development and nationwide enforcement of minimum safety and environment related performance standards for the vehicles themselves. It may well be that a basis for at least a portion. of this program is provided by the Outdoor Recreation and Land and Water Conservation Acts when considered in light of NEPA's directive that federal agencies must use "all practicable means" to improve and coordinate their policies in order to achieve environmental goals. In light of this directive, we believe that the Department should carefully consider the question of whether it might not do more to promote a unified national policy applicable to lands other than those for which the Department is directly and primarily responsible. To the extent that such a program cannot be based on existing legislative authority, we would support reasonable enabling legislation.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Seventeen
7
25
VI. Conclusion -
In closing, we should like to state that the foregoing comments should not in any way be construed as a criticism of the Department's efforts to date. In view of the magnitude of the task with which the Department was faced and the time constraints under which it has operated, we believe that the Task Force Study, the Draft Statement and the proposed regulations are an excellent work product. Even excellence can be improved upon, however, and the foregoing comments are presented to that end.
Yours very truly,
J. Gordon Arbuckle
Patton, Boggs, Blow, Verrill, Brand & May
111
Counsel for International Snowmobile Industry Association
